subject: softwareEngineering
title: GitHub Basics
description: Learn repositories, commits, branches, pull requests, forks, clones, and issues through short practical exercises.

lessons.title: Repositories and history
lessons.concept: Git tracks versions; GitHub hosts repositories and supports collaboration. A repository holds project files and revision history. A README introduces the project. A commit records a set of changes with a message and identifier. Saving or committing locally does not, by itself, upload changes to GitHub.

questions.prompt: Which tool tracks file versions locally?
questions.explanation: Git is the version-control tool; GitHub provides hosting and collaboration.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its role.
questions.explanation: Each term describes a different part of a project.

questions.prompt: Making a local commit automatically uploads it to GitHub.
questions.explanation: Committing records local history. Pushing publishes local commits to a remote.

questions.prompt: A ___ records a set of changes in project history.
questions.explanation: A commit records changes and includes a descriptive message.

lessons.title: From branch to pull request
lessons.concept: A branch lets you work separately from the default branch. For this exercise, start a branch, edit a file, commit and push the change, then open a pull request. A pull request proposes merging changes into a base branch and gives collaborators a place to discuss them. Opening it does not itself merge the change. Inspect the proposed changes before merging.

questions.explanation: Publish the branch before proposing its changes for review.

questions.prompt: Select both reasons to use a pull request.
questions.explanation: Pull requests support discussion and inspection of proposed changes.

questions.prompt: What is the full name of the GitHub feature abbreviated PR?
Before revealing: why use a separate branch?
questions.explanation: A branch keeps ongoing work separate until you integrate it.
questions.answer: To develop a change separately from the default branch and make it available for review.

lessons.title: Forks, clones, and issues
lessons.concept: A fork is a separate repository on GitHub connected to an upstream project. It can let you propose a contribution without changing the original directly. A clone downloads repository data to your computer. Issues track work such as bugs and ideas; pull requests propose code or file changes. Reporting a bug does not automatically fix or merge anything.

questions.prompt: You want a local copy of repository history. Which operation fits?
questions.explanation: Cloning downloads repository data to your computer.

questions.prompt: You found a bug but have no fix yet. What is a useful first contribution?
questions.explanation: An issue can capture a reproducible bug report for discussion.

choices.text: Open an issue describing the problem

questions.prompt: Creating a fork immediately changes the upstream project.
questions.explanation: A fork is separate; proposed changes can be offered back through a pull request.

questions.prompt: Match the action to the result.
questions.explanation: Forking, cloning, and issue tracking solve different collaboration needs.

pairs.right: Create a separate repository on GitHub
Download a repository to your computer
Record work or a bug for discussion
